ai_summary: Great Britain's total wind generation currently stands at 11.5 GW, with estimated Scottish wind output contributing 4.5 GW, representing 44.6% of installed Scottish wind capacity. Thanks to this robust renewable production, Scottish carbon intensity has dropped to 0 gCO2/kWh, standing in stark contrast to the GB-wide average of 168 gCO2/kWh. However, severe cross-border transmission constraints continue to prevent this surplus renewable power from flowing southward to major demand centers. As a result, Scottish generation curtailed so far today has reached 71.6 GWh through Balancing Mechanism bids, incurring a substantial constraint cost of about £1,943,962. To make up for this localized shortfall, thermal generators downstream had to burn an estimated 13,594,519 m³ of replacement natural gas, releasing an unnecessary 25,043 tonnes of CO2 into the atmosphere. Annualizing today's figures reveals an estimated total yearly cost of curtailment of roughly £710 million. When spread across nationwide electricity demand, this recurring inefficiency increases everybody's invoice in the UK by an estimated £2.60/MWh, highlighting how network bottlenecks inflate consumer bills while actively undermining decarbonization targets.
